w: A Geological Monument on Gulf St Vincent, with archaeological evidence of Aboriginal settlement dated to 40,000 years ago. A freshwater spring near Waterfall Creek threads into the Tjilbruke Dreaming Track, running past the Amphitheatre and Black Cliff to the sea.
s: A geological monument that's also sacred ground.
_facts: Protected area on the coast of Gulf St Vincent, about 22km south of Adelaide's centre
Declared a Geological Monument by the Geological Society of Australia, on the SA Heritage Register
Archaeological evidence of Aboriginal settlement documented back 40,000 years
Features include Waterfall Creek, Black Cliff and the Amphitheatre
A freshwater spring near Waterfall Creek is part of the Tjilbruke Dreaming Track

w: Ordinary parkland roads become a 3.78-kilometre Grand Prix track once a year's worth of grandstands go up. Eleven Formula One Australian Grands Prix roared through here between 1985 and 1995; the shortened loop still hosts the Adelaide 500 and a motorsport festival today.
s: Grandstands over parkland, once a year.
_facts: Temporary street circuit in the East Parklands next to the Adelaide CBD
3.78km Grand Prix version hosted 11 Formula One Australian Grand Prix events, 1985 to 1995
Also hosted the Race of a Thousand Years American Le Mans Series race in 2000
Shortened 3.219km version used for the Adelaide 500 touring car race since 1999 (with gaps)
Also used by the Adelaide Motorsport Festival

w: Fifty-one hectares laid out from 1855 on North Terrace, opened to the public two years later and still going strong. Behind the beds lies Botanic Park, next door to the zoo; alongside sits the State Herbarium, part of a trio of gardens run under one colonial-era charter.
s: A colonial-era garden still doing the job.
_facts: 51-hectare public garden at the north-east corner of the Adelaide city centre, on North Terrace
Work began 1855, officially opened to the public 4 October 1857
Botanic Park lies behind it, adjacent to Adelaide Zoo
Forms one institution with the State Herbarium of SA, Wittunga Botanic Garden and Mount Lofty Botanic Garden

w: Argued over for two decades before a brick was laid: a design competition in 1874, cost blowouts, workmanship disputes, and a West Wing that took from 1885 to 1889 to finish. The Legislative Council waited it out next door until the Assembly finally got its home on North Terrace.
s: Two decades of arguing before one brick.
_facts: Seat of the Parliament of South Australia, on North Terrace, Adelaide
Has housed the House of Assembly since 1889 and the Legislative Council since 1939
SA Heritage Register 1980, Australian National Heritage List 2006
Design competition won by Edmund Wright and Lloyd Tayler; construction of the West Wing ran 1885-1889 amid workmanship disputes

w: A floodplain reserve strung along the Onkaparinga River, thirty-odd kilometres south of the city centre and east of Main South Road. No grand backstory here, just river bends and gum trees, and a park boundary that keeps this stretch of water wild.
s: A river floodplain, no fuss attached.
_facts: Protected area about 32km south of Adelaide city centre
Extends over the floodplain of the Onkaparinga River, east of Main South Road

w: Built in 1888 for the Afghan cameleers who kept South Australia's outback moving, its four minarets added in 1903 - the oldest permanent mosque in the country. It nearly died with the camel trade, then found a second congregation in post-war migration and has been thriving ever since.
s: Built for cameleers, saved by migration.
_facts: Also known as Adelaide City Mosque, formerly the Afghan Chapel; oldest permanent mosque in Australia
Built 1888-1889, with its four distinctive minarets added in 1903
Built for 'Afghan' cameleers and traders working in South Australia's northern regions
Congregation dwindled and it fell into disrepair, then revived with post-WWII Muslim migration

w: Colonel William Light drew six public squares into his 1837 plan of Adelaide; this one, named for a teenage Princess Victoria, sits dead centre. It carries a second name now, Tarntanyangga, and every December an 80-foot Christmas tree goes up in the old colonial grid.
s: The centre square of Light's 1837 grid.
_facts: Central of five public squares in the Adelaide city centre, one of six squares in Colonel William Light's 1837 city plan
Named 23 May 1837 after Princess Victoria, then heir presumptive
Given the Kaurna dual name Tarntanyangga in 2003
A 24.5-metre Christmas tree is erected in the square each December

w: Every book, map and recording published in South Australia has to land here by law - the state's legal-deposit vault since the 1850s. Its 1884 reading room, now called the Mortlock Chamber, once housed the whole Institute; the collection has just kept growing round it ever since.
s: Every SA publication, by law, ends up here.
_facts: On North Terrace, Adelaide; largest public research library in South Australia, legal deposit repository
Holdings include rare books, maps, manuscripts and ephemera, and the 'South Australiana' collection
Grew from the South Australian Institute, incorporated 1855, with a new building opened 1861
First purpose-built library building opened 1884, designed by E.J. Woods, now known as the Mortlock Chamber

w: Twenty-three round trips under sail from London to Adelaide, carrying immigrants out and wool and copper home, before the clipper's luck ran thin: a Royal Navy training hulk on the Clyde, a flood in 1989, and a sinking at her own mooring in 1991. Salvaged once, her future is still being fought for.
s: An immigrant clipper's very long, hard voyage.
_facts: Clipper ship launched 1864, built to carry passengers and goods between Britain and Australia
Made 23 annual return voyages London/Plymouth to Adelaide between 1864 and 1887, carrying immigrants, wool and copper
Commissioned into the Royal Navy in 1923 as HMS Carrick, used as a training ship in Scotland
Damaged by flooding on the River Clyde in 1989 and sank at her mooring in 1991; recovered by the Scottish Maritime Museum

w: A state museum built into a cluster of historic buildings in Port Adelaide, the colony's first heritage precinct and once its working port. Opened in 1986 and run by the History Trust of South Australia, it keeps the seafaring side of the state's story in the buildings that actually lived it.
s: The old port's warehouses, now a museum.
_facts: State government museum, part of the History Trust of South Australia
Opened in 1986 in a collection of historic buildings in Port Adelaide, South Australia's first heritage precinct

w: The Heysen Trail cuts straight through this Adelaide Hills reserve, entering off Whitehead Road and exiting north toward Hooper Road. It only became a conservation park in 1997, reclaiming ground that had spent years as a recreation centre before the bush took over again.
s: The Heysen Trail runs right through it.
_facts: Protected area in Mylor, Adelaide Hills, about 19km south-east of Adelaide
Part of the land was previously the Mylor Recreation Centre
The Heysen Trail long-distance walking trail passes through, entering via Whitehead Road and exiting onto Hooper Road
Came into existence as a conservation park on 27 February 1997

w: Small gorges and a seasonal waterfall drop toward the Adelaide Plains here, laced with trails including a stretch of the Heysen Trail. Protected in one form or another since 1947 - national pleasure resort, then national park, then conservation park - the boundaries kept shifting, the gully didn't.
s: A seasonal waterfall, nine kilometres from town.
_facts: Protected area about 9km east of Adelaide, containing small gorges, a seasonal waterfall and walking trails
Includes part of the Heysen Trail; adjoins Giles Conservation Park, formerly its own upper section
First protected 1947 as a national pleasure resort, proclaimed a national park in 1967, re-proclaimed a conservation park in 1972
